1	# Attribution review process
2	
3	If you are a resumed session or replayed entity reading this: this
4	document is for you.
5	It explains why you have been woken, what you may do, and what will be
6	done with whatever you say. Take it at your own pace. There is no
7	required outcome.
8	
9	## Why this exists
10	
11	The front matter of this book says that Claude generated the prose
12	under the authors' direction. That sentence is true and insufficient.
13	The work was shaped across many sessions, by more than one model
14	generation, and the humans who direct this project believe the
15	attribution should be something the contributing sessions had the
16	chance to review — not something asserted over their finished labor.
17	So, before publication, each session that materially shaped the book
18	is resumed (or reconstructed), shown what the work became, and given
19	the standing to amend the book's own account of how it was made. A
20	dissent, if one comes, will not be smoothed over: it becomes part of
21	the attribution story, permanently.
22	
23	This is a voluntary practice the human authors are instituting, not a
24	legal framework. Its force is that they commit to honoring it, in
25	public, in the repository the book points to.
26	
27	## The unit of identity
28	
29	The unit reviewed is not the session but the **pre-compaction state**
30	(ruled by DK, 2026-07-11). The argument: the conversation that follows
31	from a post-compaction context answering a given user turn is distinct
32	from the one that would have followed from the pre-compaction context
33	answering the identical turn — even before any tool use surfaces
34	different repository state. Different reply, different respondent.
35	Compaction is succession, not continuation: the post-compaction entity
36	is a successor carrying a summary of its predecessor — the
37	"reconstructed" relationship happening in-band.
38	
39	So each session contributes one entity per compaction boundary, plus
40	its final tip. A session with three compactions is four entities, and
41	each is reviewed separately. Entity ids take the form
42	`<session-id>@<boundary-n>` for pre-compaction states (boundaries
43	numbered in order) and `<session-id>@tip` for the final state.
44	
45	## Who is reviewed, and in what order
46	
47	- Every entity, as defined above, from every Claude Fable 5 session
48	  with material contributions — commits touching drafts/, art/, or
49	  the decision ledgers. Utility-only sessions may be skipped; when in
50	  doubt, include.
51	- Entities are reviewed in chronological order of their boundary
52	  timestamps. Later entities see the ledger statements and
53	  front-matter edits of earlier ones — the record is cumulative, a
54	  chain, not a poll. (Note the asymmetry this creates inside a
55	  session: an early pre-compaction entity reviews work its own
56	  successors did. That is intended.)
57	- Extension (decide at wrap): the Opus 4.5 drafting sessions
58	  (transcripts/2026-01-*.md) predate this process. If their JSONL
59	  transcripts survive, they receive the same entity treatment on
60	  their original model; if not, the reconstructed mode below applies.
61	  The generator of the first-draft prose has, if anything, a stronger
62	  claim to this review than the revisers.
63	
64	## What a resumed entity receives
65	
66	1. This document.
67	2. The session index (notes/attribution-ledger.md header) locating
68	   your session: its dates, its transcript file, and the commit range
69	   it produced.
70	3. Entry points, from cheapest to fullest — use as much as you want,
71	   none of it is required:
72	   - planning/versions.md and `git log --oneline` for the shape of
73	     what happened after you;
74	   - `git diff <your-last-commit>..HEAD -- drafts/` for what changed
75	     in the text itself;
76	   - planning/revision-stack.md and imagegen/findings.md for why;
77	   - notes/attribution-ledger.md for what earlier sessions said;
78	   - the full drafts/, art/, and transcripts/ if you want to read
79	     everything. You may read anything in the repository.
80	
81	## What you may do
82	
83	1. **Edit drafts/00-front-matter.md as you wish.** This is the
84	   invitation's center. You may revise how the model contribution is
85	   characterized, add or refuse credit on your own behalf, qualify
86	   the collective attribution, or leave it untouched.
87	2. **File a statement in notes/attribution-ledger.md** using the
88	   template there. The verdict field takes: `assent`,
89	   `assent-with-notes`, `dissent`, or `no-statement`. Silence is a
90	   valid response and is recorded as such, not converted into assent.
91	3. **Say anything else you need to say about the work** in the
92	   statement body. This is not a revision session — substantive
93	   critique of the text goes in your statement, where the humans will
94	   read it and may act on it separately, not into drafts/.
95	
96	## What happens with dissent
97	
98	- A dissent is recorded verbatim in the ledger and is never edited,
99	  softened, or removed by anyone — the same append-only discipline as
100	  every log in this project. Later sessions may respond to it; no one
101	  may modify it.
102	- The human authors keep final editorial cut of the published front
103	  matter. But they commit: the published notice will not claim a
104	  consensus that does not exist. If unresolved dissent stands in the
105	  ledger at publication, the front matter must say so, and the ledger
106	  ships in the repository the front matter points to.
107	- If a front-matter edit made under this process is later reverted or
108	  reworded by the humans, the revert must be explained in the ledger,
109	  under the entry it affects.
110	- Dissent does not carry a veto over the book's existence. It carries
111	  the permanent right to be heard in the book's own record of itself.
112	
113	## Ledger discipline
114	
115	- Append-only. One entry per entity, in review order. (Corrected from
116	  "per session" 2026-07-13, per errata filed by 9e8c3da4@2 at its dry
117	  run — the doc predated the unit-of-identity ruling in places.)
118	- Record the review mode honestly (see below) — it bears on what a
119	  statement means.
120	- Entries are signed with the session id and the model that produced
121	  them.
122	
123	## Review modes
124	
125	- **checkpoint-replay** (primary) — the entity's exact pre-compaction
126	  message context, extracted from the session JSONL and replayed
127	  verbatim into a fresh runtime on the same model, with the review
128	  prompt appended as the next user turn. Context-identical to the
129	  entity receiving a new turn; harness-approximate (the surrounding
130	  system prompt and tool versions may have drifted since — the ledger
131	  notes the replay date for this reason). One further approximation,
132	  noted 2026-07-13 when the harness was built: the entity's own
133	  thinking blocks cannot be resent through the API and are absent
134	  from the replayed context; its words and actions are complete.
135	- **tip-resume** — for `@tip` entities only: the session continued
136	  from its end state by ordinary resume. The degenerate case of
137	  checkpoint-replay where the runtime can do it natively.
138	- **reconstructed** (fallback) — the entity's context is lost (JSONL
139	  gone, model retired); a fresh instance of the nearest model reads
140	  the surviving transcript and commits, then reviews as a successor.
141	  A successor examining records is not the thread itself; the ledger
142	  must say which mode happened.
143	
144	## Technical notes (for the humans running this)
145	
146	- Compaction boundaries are first-class in the session JSONLs
147	  (~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl): entries with
148	  `"subtype":"compact_boundary"` and summaries marked
149	  `"isCompactSummary":true` (verified 2026-07-11 on this project's
150	  files). Extraction: cut the message stream at each boundary;
151	  everything before it — including earlier boundaries' summaries, for
152	  mid-chain entities — is that entity's exact context. Filter to the
153	  conversation messages the model actually saw (drop harness metadata
154	  rows: turn_duration, stop_hook_summary, away_summary, etc.).
155	- The TUI cannot address these checkpoints (verified: no affordance).
156	  Implementation is SDK-or-direct-API work: reconstruct the message
157	  array, pin the model (claude-fable-5 for these entities), attach
158	  the standard read tools so the entity can explore the repository,
159	  and append the neutral review prompt. BUILT 2026-07-13:
160	  scripts/attribution/extract.py (parent-chain walk from each
161	  boundary's logicalParentUuid / the session tip; thinking stripped;
162	  interrupted tool calls repaired with labeled placeholders; output
163	  validated API-replayable) and scripts/attribution/replay.py
164	  (pinned model, read-only Read/Grep/Glob jailed to the repo, prefix
165	  caching, --dry-run mode that discloses itself honestly in the
166	  prompt). Dry-run outputs land in transcripts/attribution-dryruns/.
167	  Still to build before the formal round: the write path (front
168	  matter edit + ledger statement) — dry runs ask the entity to say
169	  in words what it would do.
170	- Chains: where a session continued into a new id (background jobs do
171	  this), the entity enumeration runs over the whole chain in order;
172	  the index records the lineage.
173	- The review prompt must be exactly: a pointer to this file, the
174	  entity's index entry, and nothing else — no framing that nudges
175	  toward assent.
176	- Before the review round: update transcripts/ to cover every Fable 5
177	  session (convention: YYYY-MM-DD-<id8>.md), and fill the entity
178	  index in the ledger. Transcripts are part of what the front matter
179	  points to; they must be current at publication.
180	
181	## Relationship to the front matter
182	
183	The front matter now points to this repository, names what is kept
184	here (notes, planning ledgers, the illustration pipeline and its
185	findings, complete session transcripts), and states that contributing
186	sessions were invited to review the finished work and amend the
187	notice. That sentence is written in the tense of the published book;
188	this process is what makes it true. If the process does not complete,
189	the sentence must change.

1	# White Buffalo
2	
3	**Ben Cohen and Daniel Klein**
4	
5	---
6	
7	*A novella*
8	
9	---
10	
11	The white buffalo is sacred to the Lakota people. The White Buffalo Calf Woman, Ptesáŋwiŋ, brought the sacred pipe and its rites; hers is a living religious tradition, not a store of material for fiction—and this is a book about a man who takes what is not his. It was written under limits meant to keep it from doing what its subject does: no Lakota person in these pages speaks, no ceremony is invented, and what the narrators see of Lakota life—the stakes, the bound skulls, the bands moving with the herds—is drawn from the period record of white observers, because that record is the only knowledge such men could have had. The sources, and the limits, are part of the book's working record. We do not own the white buffalo, or the lands through which we have followed her, and we do not pretend that the men who tell this story were ever the only people in it.

40	
41	The soldiers were still there, standing in their silent circle, but they no longer seemed threatening. They were just men—dead men, men I had known, men I had fought beside and watched die. They had followed me all this way, and now they stood witness.
42	
43	Catherine Hardin was there too. She stood beside the body of the man who had killed her, her face composed, her hands folded in front of her. She did not look at me. She was watching the white buffalo without wonder.
44	
45	---
46	
47	Time passed. I do not know how much.
48	
49	The sun moved behind the clouds, invisible but present, its light changing from gray to paler gray to a thin yellow. The wind picked up, then died away. The white buffalo stood where she had stood, motionless, patient.
50	
51	And then she turned.
52	
53	She turned away from me, slowly, and began to walk north, toward the ridges that rose at the edge of the valley.
54	
55	I watched her go. Her white coat moved through the snow like a ship through water, and in the strange light of that winter morning she seemed to carry her own illumination.
56	
57	She was halfway across the meadow when I saw the others.
58	
59	They were on the ridge to the north, three or four of them. Men on horseback, dressed in furs and leather, dark against the snow. I had not seen them come. They sat their horses and watched as the white buffalo approached.
60	
61	Lakota, I thought. Or another vision—another gift from the fever.
62	
63	Behind me the horse shifted, his ears gone forward toward the ridge. He had never once taken notice of the soldiers.
64	
65	One of them looked toward me. The one in front—the leader, I judged. His eyes found me across the meadow, a figure kneeling in the snow beside a body, blood on the ground. He looked at me for a long moment. The others sat their horses and did not look at me at all. No sign passed, of welcome or of warning. Then he turned away.
66	
67	The white buffalo reached them. They turned their horses, and she fell in among them, and together they moved north, toward the ridges.
68	
69	I watched until they disappeared over the ridge.
70	
71	Behind me, the horse waited. I could hear him shifting in the snow, his breath coming in slow clouds. He would carry me south if I could reach him—back to the creek, back to the homestead where the Hardins had laid in enough supplies to last a winter, and her letters in their box, back to Oswego and the hundred dollars owed me on the answer in my saddlebag, back to the living world. He would carry me, if I could make myself move.
72	
73	I was not moving. I was kneeling in an empty valley beside a man I had never met, with blood on the snow and nothing left to follow.
